title: Per Pallanteum. Venus et Volcanus
titleEn: Evander's Walk and Vulcan's Promise — Aeneid VIII.306–406
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The rites of Hercules are over, and the company walks back to the town. Old Evander keeps Aeneas and his own son Pallas beside him and lightens the way with talk, and Aeneas, delighted, asks about everything he sees. Evander tells the story of the place: woodland once held by Fauns and Nymphs and a wild race of men born from tree-trunks, until Saturn, driven from heaven by Jupiter, came and hid here, gave them laws and named the land Latium, and ruled a Golden Age that sank by degrees into greed and war; then came new peoples and kings, the river took a new name, and last of all Evander himself, an exile brought here by fate and his prophetic mother Carmentis. Then he shows the sights, and they are the sights of Rome before Rome: the Carmental Gate, the grove Romulus would make his Asylum, the cave of the Lupercal, the Argiletum, the Tarpeian Rock and the Capitol, golden in Virgil's day and thorn-scrub in Evander's, where a god, perhaps Jupiter, is felt to dwell; the ruins of two towns on the Janiculum and the Capitol; cattle lowing where the Forum and the smart quarter of the Carinae would stand. At his humble house Evander bids his guest dare to despise riches, as Hercules did, and gives him a bed of leaves and a bearskin. Night falls. Venus, afraid for her son, goes to her husband Vulcan in their golden bedroom and, as Thetis and Aurora did before her for Achilles and Memnon, asks him to forge arms for Aeneas; she wins him with an embrace, and he promises all that fire and his art can do. The arms he makes will be the shield of Book VIII's close.

sentences.t:
Exim se cuncti divinis rebus ad urbem
perfectis referunt.
sentences.l:
Thereupon they all, the divine things being finished, to the city
betake themselves.
sentences.i: Then, the sacred rites completed, they all made their way back to the city.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'Exim', an old form of 'exinde', 'thereupon'. 'divinis rebus… perfectis', ablative absolute, 'the divine business having been completed', the rites at the Ara Maxima that closed the last part, split across the line around 'ad urbem'. 'se… referunt', 'they carry themselves back', 'return', with 'cuncti', 'all of them', the Arcadians and the Trojans together. 'ad urbem', Evander's town of Pallanteum on the Palatine. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ibat rex obsitus aevo
et comitem Aenean iuxta natumque tenebat
ingrediens varioque viam sermone levabat.
sentences.l:
Went the king, beset with age,
and as companion Aeneas close by and his son he kept
as he walked, and with varied the way talk he lightened.
sentences.i: The king walked on, weighed down with years, keeping Aeneas and his son close beside him as he went, and lightened the road with talk of many things.
sentences.n: 'Ibat', 'was going', the imperfect of a scene in progress, like 'tenebat' and 'levabat' after it. 'obsitus aevo', 'overgrown with age', from 'obsero', 'to sow over', 'to cover': age has spread over him like a crop. 'comitem', predicative, 'as his companion'. 'Aenean', the Greek accusative of 'Aeneas'; 'Ae-' is one long syllable, and the '-em' of 'comitem' is elided before it. 'natum', Evander's son Pallas (8.104). 'iuxta', adverb, 'close by'. 'ingrediens', 'walking', 'as he went'. 'varioque… sermone', 'with varied talk', framing 'viam', 'the road', which he 'lightens', makes seem shorter. Elision 'comit(em) Aenean'.

sentences.t:
miratur facilisque oculos fert omnia circum
Aeneas capiturque locis et singula laetus
exquiritque auditque virum monimenta priorum.
sentences.l:
Marvels and his ready eyes he carries all things round,
Aeneas, and is captivated by the places, and each thing, glad,
both asks about and hears, of men the memorials of former.
sentences.i: Aeneas was full of wonder, and turned his quick eyes on everything about him; the places held him spellbound, and he gladly asked about each thing in turn and listened to the stories of the men of old.
sentences.n: The print has 'miratur', lowercase after the full stop that ends 309, a misprint for 'Miratur', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i begin with a capital. 'Miratur', 'marvels', placed first, with its subject 'Aeneas' held back to the start of the next line. 'facilis… oculos', accusative plural in '-is', 'ready', 'easily moving' eyes, eyes that turn wherever they are drawn. 'omnia circum', 'round all things', the preposition after its noun (anastrophe). 'capitur… locis', 'is taken', 'charmed', by the places, 'locis' ablative of means. 'singula', 'each thing', object of both verbs; 'exquiritque auditque', 'both asks and hears', the double '-que'. 'virum… priorum', 'of earlier men', framing 'monimenta', 'memorials', in apposition to 'singula'; 'virum' = 'virorum', the old short genitive plural. Elisions 'facilisqu(e) oculos', 'exquiritqu(e) auditque'.

sentences.t: Tum rex Euandrus, Romanae conditor arcis:
sentences.l: Then King Evander, of the Roman the founder citadel:
sentences.i: Then King Evander, who founded the citadel of Rome, spoke:
sentences.n: The verb of speaking is left out, as often before a speech ('Aeolus haec contra'). 'Euandrus', Greenough's spelling of the Greek name, Euandros, 'good man'; the Greek 'eu' is one syllable, 'Eu-an-drus'. 'Romanae conditor arcis', 'founder of the Roman citadel', framing 'conditor': Evander's town stood on the Palatine, and Virgil calls him its founder with Rome's future in view. There is a point in it: the first 'conditor' of the Roman citadel is a Greek exile. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Haec nemora indigenae fauni nymphaeque tenebant
gensque virum truncis et duro robore nata,
quis neque mos neque cultus erat, nec iungere tauros
aut componere opes norant aut parcere parto,
sed rami atque asper victu venatus alebat.
sentences.l:
“These groves the native Fauns and Nymphs held,
and a race of men from trunks and from hard oak born,
to whom neither custom nor cultivation was, nor to yoke bulls
or to store up wealth did they know, or to spare what was got,
but boughs and, harsh in its fare, hunting nourished them.
sentences.i: “These woods were once the home of native Fauns and Nymphs, and of a race of men sprung from tree-trunks and hard oak, who had no settled ways and no tilling of the soil; they did not know how to yoke the ox, or lay up wealth, or husband what they had gained, but lived on what the branches bore and on the hard fare of the hunt.
sentences.n: Evander's speech opens (314–336). 'indigenae', 'native', with both 'fauni' and 'nymphae': the Fauns, Italian woodland spirits, are here a whole people. 'gensque virum', 'a race of men' ('virum' = 'virorum' again). 'truncis et duro robore nata', 'born from trunks and hard oak': men sprung from trees is an old story (Penelope tells the disguised Odysseus he was not born 'from an oak or a rock', Odyssey 19, from memory). 'quis' = 'quibus', dative of possession with 'erat', 'who had'. 'mos', settled custom; 'cultus', tillage. 'norant' = 'noverant', 'knew how', with three infinitives. 'componere opes', 'to store up wealth'; 'parcere parto', 'to spare what was gained' ('parto', from 'pario', 'get'). 'rami', 'boughs', meaning the acorns and berries they bore; 'asper victu venatus', 'hunting harsh in its food', 'victu' ablative of respect. Elisions 'nemor(a) indigenae', 'componer(e) opes', 'ram(i) atque', 'atqu(e) asper'.

sentences.t:
Primus ab aetherio venit Saturnus Olympo,
arma Iovis fugiens et regnis exsul ademptis.
sentences.l:
First from heavenly came Saturn Olympus,
the arms of Jupiter fleeing and, his realms taken away, an exile.
sentences.i: The first to come was Saturn, down from the heights of Olympus, fleeing the weapons of Jupiter, an exile stripped of his kingdom.
sentences.n: 'Primus', 'first', the first civiliser. 'aetherio… Olympo', 'from heavenly Olympus', enclosing 'venit Saturnus', ablative of the place from which with 'ab'. 'Saturnus', the old Italian god identified with the Greek Kronos, whom his son Zeus (Jupiter) overthrew; the Romans told that the exiled god came to Italy. 'arma Iovis fugiens', 'fleeing the arms of Jupiter'. 'regnis… ademptis', ablative absolute, 'his realms having been taken from him'; 'exsul', 'an exile', in apposition to the subject. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Is genus indocile ac dispersum montibus altis
composuit legesque dedit Latiumque vocari
maluit, his quoniam latuisset tutis in oris.
sentences.l:
He the race unteachable and scattered on the mountains high
brought together and laws gave, and Latium to be called
preferred, since he had lain hid, safe, in these shores.
sentences.i: He gathered that untamed race, scattered over the high mountains, and gave them laws, and chose to call the land Latium, because he had lain hidden safe within its borders.
sentences.n: The print has 'tutis', a misprint for 'tutus', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. The ablative plural 'tutis' has a long '-is', which the fifth foot cannot take ('tū-tŭs ĭn | ō-rīs'); 'tutus' is the Latin Library's reading, and the line is scanned with it (as 'vidit' for the print's 'videt' at 6.684). 'Is', 'he', Saturn. 'genus indocile ac dispersum', 'the unteachable and scattered race', the men of 315. 'composuit', 'put together', settled them in a community, picking up 'componere' (317). 'Latiumque vocari maluit', 'and preferred that (the land) be called Latium'. The name is explained from 'latuisset', 'he had lain hidden', from 'lateo': an ancient etymology. The subjunctive gives the reason as Saturn's own thought. 'his… in oris', 'in these shores'; 'tutus', 'safe', goes with Saturn. Elision 'indocil(e) ac'.

sentences.t:
Aurea quae perhibent illo sub rege fuere
saecula.
sentences.l:
Golden, which they tell of, under that king were
the ages.
sentences.i: Under that king were the golden ages that men tell of.
sentences.n: 'Aurea… saecula', 'the golden ages', framing the sentence across the line, with 'saecula' held back to the start of 325 for weight. 'quae perhibent', 'which they speak of', 'which people tell of', a relative clause set between 'Aurea' and its noun; 'aurea' can also be taken inside it, 'the ages they call golden'. 'illo sub rege', 'under that king', the preposition between adjective and noun. 'fuere' = 'fuerunt', the '-ere' perfect. The Golden Age under Saturn (Kronos) is Hesiod's (Works and Days, from memory); Virgil makes Italy its home, and in Book VI Anchises promises that Augustus will bring it back to Latium (6.792–794). No elisions.

sentences.t:
Sic placida populos in pace regebat,
deterior donec paulatim ac decolor aetas
et belli rabies et amor successit habendi.
sentences.l:
Thus in tranquil the peoples in peace he ruled,
until a worse little by little and discoloured age
and of war the madness and the love came after of possessing.
sentences.i: So he ruled his peoples in untroubled peace, until little by little a worse and tarnished age came on, and the madness of war, and the love of gain.
sentences.n: 'Sic', 'in this way', with laws and settled life. 'placida… in pace', 'in calm peace', framing 'populos'. 'regebat', imperfect, the long reign. 'deterior… ac decolor aetas', 'a worse and discoloured age', the metal of the Golden Age growing dull and base. 'donec', 'until', with the perfect indicative 'successit', 'came after', 'took its place'; the verb is singular, agreeing with the nearest of its three subjects. 'belli rabies', 'the madness of war'. 'amor… habendi', 'the love of having', 'habendi' the genitive of the gerund, framing 'successit'. The three subjects grow from a dull age to frenzy and greed. Elision 'paulat(im) ac'.

sentences.t:
Tum manus Ausonia et gentes venere Sicanae,
saepius et nomen posuit Saturnia tellus;
sentences.l:
Then a band Ausonian and peoples came Sicanian,
and more often its name laid aside the Saturnian land;
sentences.i: Then came the Ausonian bands and the Sicanian peoples, and again and again the land of Saturn put off its name;
sentences.n: 'manus Ausonia', 'the Ausonian band', the Ausones, an old people of central and southern Italy, whose name poets use for Italy as a whole. 'gentes… Sicanae', 'the Sicanian peoples', thought to have lived in Italy before they crossed to Sicily. 'venere' = 'venerunt'. 'saepius', 'more often', 'again and again': each new people renamed the land, so that it was Saturnia, Ausonia, Hesperia, Oenotria, Italia in turn. 'posuit nomen', 'laid aside its name'. 'Saturnia tellus', 'the land of Saturn', a name for Italy (as in Georgics 2, from memory). Elision 'Ausoni(a) et'.

sentences.i: then came kings, and fierce Thybris of giant frame, after whom we Italians have since called our river Thybris, and the old Albula lost its true name;
sentences.n: 'tum reges', 'then (came) kings', the verb carried over from 'venere'. 'asperque immani corpore Thybris', 'and Thybris, fierce, of huge body', 'immani corpore' an ablative of description. Thybris is here a king who gave his name to the Tiber (Livy tells of a king of Alba, Tiberinus, drowned in the river, from memory). 'a quo… cognomine', 'from whom as a name', 'after whom'. 'Itali… diximus', 'we Italians called': Evander, though a Greek, counts himself among the Italians. 'fluvium… Thybrim', 'the river (as) Thybris', a predicate accusative, with the accusative in '-im', as in 'Tiberim'. 'amisit… Albula nomen', 'Albula lost its name', with no connective (asyndeton): 'Albula', 'the whitish', was the river's older name. 'verum vetus', 'its true, old (name)'. Elision 'asperqu(e) immani'.

sentences.t:
me pulsum patria pelagique extrema sequentem
Fortuna omnipotens et ineluctabile fatum
his posuere locis matrisque egere tremenda
Carmentis nymphae monita et deus auctor Apollo.
sentences.l:
Me, driven from my fatherland and of the sea the furthest bounds following,
Fortune all-powerful and inescapable fate
in these placed places, and of my mother drove me the dread
Carmentis, the nymph, warnings, and the god, my sponsor, Apollo.”
sentences.i: As for me, driven from my homeland and following the sea to its furthest bounds, all-powerful Fortune and inescapable fate set me down in this place, and I was urged on by the dread warnings of my mother, the nymph Carmentis, and by the authority of the god Apollo.”
sentences.n: The print has no closing mark after 'Apollo.' at the end of 336, a misprint for 'Apollo.”', corrected here: the speech begun at 314 ends at 336, as 'Vix ea dicta' (337) shows; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i close the speech. 'me', object of 'posuere' and 'egere', put first: Evander comes last in his history. 'pulsum patria', 'driven from my country', ablative of separation; 'pelagique extrema', 'and the sea's furthest bounds'. 'ineluctabile', 'not to be wrestled free of' ('in-' + 'eluctor'). 'posuere', 'egere', '-ere' perfects, 'egere' 'drove (me)'. 'matris… tremenda… Carmentis nymphae monita', 'the awe-inspiring warnings of my mother, the nymph Carmentis', 'Carmentis' genitive (nominative also 'Carmenta'), Evander's prophetess-mother. 'deus auctor Apollo', 'Apollo, the god, as sponsor', the authority behind the venture. Elisions 'pelagiqu(e) extrema', 'Fortun(a) omnipotens', 'matrisqu(e) egere', 'monit(a) et'.

sentences.t: Vix ea dicta:
sentences.l: Scarcely these things said:
sentences.i: Scarcely had he spoken these words,
sentences.n: 'Vix ea dicta', 'scarcely (were) these things said', with 'sunt' or 'erant' left out, a common formula of transition: no sooner had he finished than he was on the move. 'ea', neuter plural, 'these things', the words of the speech. Here 'dehinc', which follows, has its two syllables, 'de-hinc' (at 1.131 Virgil makes it one). No elisions.

sentences.t:
dehinc progressus monstrat et aram
et Carmentalem Romani nomine portam
quam memorant, nymphae priscum Carmentis honorem,
vatis fatidicae, cecinit quae prima futuros
Aeneadas magnos et nobile Pallanteum.
sentences.l:
then going forward he shows both the altar
and the Carmental, by the Romans by name, gate,
which they call so, of the nymph the ancient honour, Carmentis,
the prophesying seer, who sang first of the future
Aeneadae, great, and noble Pallanteum.
sentences.i: when he moved on and showed him the altar and the gate the Romans call the Carmental Gate, an ancient tribute to the nymph Carmentis, the seer who spoke the future, who first foretold the greatness of the sons of Aeneas and the glory of Pallanteum.
sentences.n: 'dehinc', 'then'; 'progressus', 'moving on'. 'monstrat… et aram et… portam', 'shows both the altar and the gate': the altar of Carmentis and the Porta Carmentalis, a gate in the old wall of Rome at the foot of the Capitol. 'Carmentalem Romani nomine portam quam memorant', 'the gate the Romans call Carmental by name': 'Romani' and 'nomine' belong to the relative clause but stand before 'quam', inside 'Carmentalem… portam'. 'priscum… honorem', 'ancient honour', in apposition: the gate is her monument. 'vatis fatidicae', 'the fate-speaking seer', in apposition to 'Carmentis'; her name was linked with 'carmen', 'song', 'prophecy'. 'futuros Aeneadas magnos', 'the Aeneadae, great to be', Aeneas's descendants, the Romans; 'Aeneadas' is 'Ae-nĕ-a-das', 'Ae-' one syllable. 'Pallanteum', Evander's town, named after his ancestor Pallas (8.51–54), is four syllables, 'Pal-lan-tē-um', with a spondee in the fifth foot, a weighty Greek line-ending. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Hinc lucum ingentem quem Romulus acer Asylum
rettulit et gelida monstrat sub rupe Lupercal,
Parrhasio dictum Panos de more Lycaei.
sentences.l:
Hence a grove huge, which Romulus the fierce into an Asylum
turned, and under the cold rock he shows the Lupercal,
named after the Parrhasian custom of Lycaean Pan.
sentences.i: Next he shows the great grove that fiery Romulus made into a sanctuary, and under the chill rock the Lupercal, named after the fashion of Arcadia for Pan of Mount Lycaeus.
sentences.n: 'Hinc', 'next'. 'lucum ingentem', like 'Lupercal', object of 'monstrat' (343). 'quem Romulus acer Asylum rettulit', 'which bold Romulus made into an Asylum': Romulus opened a refuge on the Capitol for outlaws and runaways, to people his city (Livy 1, from memory). 'rettulit' is taken here as 'made over into'; others take it as 'restored'. 'gelida… sub rupe', 'under the cold rock', the cave below the Palatine where the she-wolf suckled the twins. 'Lupercal', the shrine of the Luperci, whose February rite was Rome's own. 'Parrhasio… de more', 'after the Parrhasian (= Arcadian) custom', interlaced with 'Panos… Lycaei', 'of Lycaean Pan', 'Panos' the Greek genitive of 'Pan': Pan was worshipped on Mount Lycaeus in Arcadia, and 'Lycaeus' was linked with Greek 'lykos', 'wolf', as 'Lupercal' with Latin 'lupus'. 'dictum', 'named', agrees with 'Lupercal'. Elision 'luc(um) ingentem'.

sentences.t:
Nec non et sacri monstrat nemus Argileti
testaturque locum et letum docet hospitis Argi.
sentences.l:
And also of the sacred he shows the grove, of Argiletum,
and calls the place to witness, and of the death tells of his guest Argus.
sentences.i: He shows him too the grove of the holy Argiletum, and calls the place to witness, and tells how Argus, once his guest, met his death.
sentences.n: 'Nec non et', 'and not not, also', 'and also', a strengthened connective. 'sacri… nemus Argileti', 'the grove of the sacred Argiletum', enclosing 'monstrat nemus'; the Argiletum was later a street of booksellers running down into the Forum. The name was explained as 'Argi letum', 'the death of Argus', and that etymology is what 346 acts out. The story (told by Servius, from memory) was that Argus, a guest of Evander, plotted against him and was killed by Evander's men without his knowledge; Evander buried him and made the place sacred. 'testatur locum', 'calls the place to witness', that he had no part in the killing of a guest, a grave crime. 'hospitis Argi', 'of his guest Argus'. 'sacri' has its first syllable long before 'cr', and the line ends in a spondaic fifth foot, 'Ar-gī', before 'lē-tī'. Elision 'loc(um) et'.

sentences.t:
Hinc ad Tarpeiam sedem et Capitolia ducit,
aurea nunc, olim silvestribus horrida dumis.
sentences.l:
Hence to the Tarpeian seat and the Capitol he leads,
golden now, once with woodland bristling thickets.
sentences.i: From there he leads him to the Tarpeian seat and the Capitol, golden now, but then rough with tangled woodland thorn.
sentences.n: 'Tarpeiam sedem', 'the Tarpeian seat', the Capitoline, named for Tarpeia, who betrayed the citadel to the Sabines; from the Tarpeian Rock traitors were later thrown. 'Capitolia', the poetic plural, the hill of Jupiter's great temple. 'aurea nunc', 'golden now', in Virgil's own day, when the temple of Jupiter had a gilded roof; 'olim', 'once', in Evander's. 'silvestribus horrida dumis', 'bristling with woodland thickets', 'horrida' from 'horreo', 'stand on end', of a rough, shaggy surface. The contrast of then and now runs through the whole walk; this line puts it most plainly. Elision 'sed(em) et'.

sentences.t:
Iam tum religio pavidos terrebat agrestis
dira loci, iam tum silvam saxumque tremebant.
sentences.l:
Already then religious awe the timid terrified rustics,
dread, of the place; already then the wood and the rock they trembled at.
sentences.i: Even then the dread holiness of the place struck fear into the timid country people; even then they trembled at that wood and that rock.
sentences.n: 'Iam tum… iam tum', 'already then… already then', anaphora: the place was holy before there was a temple on it. 'religio… dira loci', 'the dread sanctity of the place', 'religio' the sense of a divine presence and the awe it brings, split across the line from 'dira'. 'pavidos… agrestis', 'the timid country folk', accusative plural in '-is', framing 'terrebat'. 'tremebant', 'they trembled at', transitive, with 'silvam saxumque' as object: the wood and the Tarpeian rock. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Hoc nemus, hunc, inquit, frondoso vertice collem
(quis deus incertum est) habitat deus:
sentences.l:
“This grove, this, he says, with leafy summit, hill
(which god is uncertain) inhabits a god:
sentences.i: “This grove,” he said, “this hill with its leafy crown, is the dwelling of a god, though which god no one knows;
sentences.n: Evander speaks again. Greenough sets 'inquit', 'he says', inside the speech without closing and reopening the speech marks, his habit (7.594 'inquit', 8.122 'ait'); read 'Hoc nemus, hunc,” inquit, “frondoso…'. 'Hoc nemus, hunc… collem', 'this grove, this hill', both objects of 'habitat', 'inhabits'. 'frondoso vertice', 'with leafy top', ablative of description. '(quis deus incertum est)', 'which god it is is uncertain', an indirect question with the verb left out, set in parentheses. 'habitat deus', 'a god dwells (here)', the noun repeated from the parenthesis. Seneca quotes 'quis deus incertum est, habitat deus' of the god who dwells in every good man (Letter 41, from memory). Elision 'incert(um) est'.

sentences.t:
Arcades ipsum
credunt se vidisse Iovem, cum saepe nigrantem
aegida concuteret dextra nimbosque cieret.
sentences.l:
the Arcadians himself
believe they have seen Jupiter, when often the darkening
aegis he shook with his right hand and storm-clouds roused.
sentences.i: the Arcadians believe they have seen Jupiter himself, often, shaking the dark aegis in his right hand and stirring up the storm-clouds.
sentences.n: 'Arcades', 'the Arcadians', Evander's people. 'ipsum… Iovem', 'Jupiter himself', framing 'credunt se vidisse', 'believe that they have seen', accusative and infinitive. 'cum saepe… concuteret… cieret', 'when he often shook… and roused', 'cum' with the imperfect subjunctive of the circumstances. 'nigrantem aegida', 'the darkening aegis', 'aegida' a Greek accusative; the aegis is the storm-shield of Zeus in Homer, which he shakes to send thunder and terror (Iliad 17, from memory). 'dextra', ablative, 'with his right hand'. 'nimbos', 'storm-clouds'. The hill will be the Capitol, and the god Capitoline Jupiter. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Haec duo praeterea disiectis oppida muris,
reliquias veterumque vides monimenta virorum.
sentences.l:
These two besides, with thrown-down walls, towns,
remnants and of men of old you see the memorials.
sentences.i: These two towns, too, with their walls in ruins, are what you see left of men of old, their remains and their memorials.
sentences.n: 'Haec duo… oppida', 'these two towns', framing 'praeterea disiectis', with 'disiectis… muris', ablative of description, 'with walls thrown down'. 'disiectis' is 'dis-iec-tis', the 'i' after the prefix a consonant. 'reliquias… monimenta', in apposition to 'oppida', 'as remains and memorials'; 'vides', 'you see', the guest addressed directly. 'reliquias' has its first syllable long (often spelled 'relliquias'), 'rē-li-qui-as'. 'veterum… virorum', 'of men of old', framing the clause. No elisions.

sentences.t: Hanc Ianus pater, hanc Saturnus condidit arcem:
sentences.l: This father Janus, this Saturn founded citadel:
sentences.i: One of these citadels father Janus founded, the other Saturn:
sentences.n: 'Hanc… hanc', 'this one… that one', anaphora, both with 'arcem', 'citadel', held to the end. 'Ianus pater', 'father Janus', the old Italian god of gates and beginnings, two-faced, here an early king of the land. 'Saturnus', the god of 319. 'condidit', singular, with each subject in turn. No elisions.

sentences.t: Ianiculum huic, illi fuerat Saturnia nomen.”
sentences.l: Janiculum to the one, to the other had been Saturnia the name.”
sentences.i: Janiculum was the name of the one, and Saturnia of the other.”
sentences.n: 'huic… illi', 'to this one… to that one', datives of possession with 'fuerat… nomen', 'had been the name'. The Janiculum, named for Janus, is the ridge across the Tiber; Saturnia, Saturn's town, was the old name given to a settlement on the Capitol. 'fuerat', pluperfect, 'had been', before it fell into ruin. Evander's speech ends here, and Greenough closes the mark. Elision 'Ianicul(um) huic'.

sentences.t:
Talibus inter se dictis ad tecta subibant
pauperis Euandri passimque armenta videbant
Romanoque foro et lautis mugire Carinis.
sentences.l:
With such among themselves words, to the house they came up,
of poor Evander, and everywhere herds they saw
lowing in the Roman Forum and in the elegant Carinae.
sentences.i: Talking in this way among themselves they drew near to the house of Evander, a poor man, and saw cattle everywhere, lowing in what would be the Roman Forum and the fine streets of the Carinae.
sentences.n: 'Talibus inter se dictis', ablative absolute, 'such things being said among them'. 'ad tecta subibant', 'were coming up to the house', 'tecta', 'roofs', for the dwelling. 'pauperis Euandri', 'of poor Evander', at the head of the line: the king is poor, and that is his glory (see 364–365). 'Euandri' has 'Eu-' as one syllable. 'passim', 'everywhere', 'here and there'. 'armenta… mugire', accusative and infinitive with 'videbant', 'saw herds lowing'. 'Romano… foro', 'in the Roman Forum', 'et lautis… Carinis', 'and in the elegant Carinae', locative ablatives: the Carinae, 'the Keels', was a smart residential quarter on the slope of the Esquiline in Virgil's time. The cattle graze where the centre of the world's capital will stand. Elisions 'passimqu(e) armenta', 'for(o) et'.

sentences.t:
Ut ventum ad sedes: “Haec, inquit, limina victor
Alcides subiit, haec illum regia cepit.
sentences.l:
When it was come to the dwelling: “This, he says, threshold the victor
Alcides entered, this him palace received.
sentences.i: When they reached the house he said: “Through this door Alcides passed in his triumph; this palace took him in.
sentences.n: 'Ut ventum ad sedes', 'when it was come to the dwelling', the impersonal passive 'ventum (est)', 'they came', with the auxiliary left out. Again Greenough keeps 'inquit' inside the speech marks; read '“Haec,” inquit, “limina…'. 'Haec… limina', 'this threshold', plural for singular. 'victor', 'victorious', fresh from killing Cacus. 'Alcides', 'descendant of Alcaeus', Hercules. 'subiit', 'came under', 'entered', its last syllable long, the old long '-īt' of the perfect (from '-ivit'). 'haec… regia', 'this palace', said of a humble house: the greatest of heroes was content with it. Elision 'vent(um) ad'.

sentences.t:
Aude, hospes, contemnere opes et te quoque dignum
finge deo rebusque veni non asper egenis.”
sentences.l:
Dare, guest, to despise wealth, and yourself also worthy
fashion of the god, and to our affairs come not harsh, needy.”
sentences.i: Have the courage, my guest, to hold riches cheap; shape yourself too to be worthy of the god, and do not look with scorn on our poor estate.”
sentences.n: A famous couplet, quoted more than once by Seneca (Letters 18 and 31, from memory). 'Aude… contemnere opes', 'dare to despise wealth', 'aude' imperative of 'audeo'. 'hospes', 'guest', vocative. 'te quoque dignum finge deo', 'mould yourself too (as) worthy of the god', 'deo' ablative with 'dignum'; the god is Hercules, who entered this house, and who won his godhead by toil. 'rebus… egenis', 'to our needy circumstances', dative with 'non asper' (or with 'veni', 'come to'); 'veni' is the imperative of 'venio'. 'non asper', 'not harsh', not disdainful, an understatement. Evander's speech ends, and Greenough closes the mark. Elisions 'Aud(e) hospes', 'contemner(e) opes'.

sentences.t:
dixit et angusti subter fastigia tecti
ingentem Aenean duxit stratisque locavit
effultum foliis et pelle Libystidis ursae.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and of his narrow beneath the gables house
the huge Aeneas he led, and on strewn placed him
supported, leaves and the hide of a Libyan she-bear.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and under the roof-beams of his narrow house he led the mighty Aeneas, and set him to rest on a bed of strewn leaves and the hide of a Libyan bear.
sentences.n: The print has 'dixit', lowercase after the full stop and closing mark that end 365, a misprint for 'Dixit', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source; l and i begin with a capital. 'angusti… tecti', 'of the narrow house', framing 'subter fastigia', 'beneath the gables', with the preposition 'subter' before its noun. 'ingentem Aenean', 'huge Aeneas', set against 'angusti': the hero is too big for the poor house, and the house is the better for it. 'Aenean' again 'Ae-ne-an', the '-em' of 'ingentem' elided before it. 'stratis… foliis', 'on strewn leaves', with 'effultum', 'propped up', 'resting' (from 'effulcio'). 'pelle Libystidis ursae', 'the skin of a Libyan she-bear', 'Libystis', '-idis', a Greek feminine adjective. Elision 'ingent(em) Aenean'.

sentences.t: Nox ruit et fuscis tellurem amplectitur alis.
sentences.l: Night rushes on and with dusky the earth embraces wings.
sentences.i: Night came rushing in and held the earth in the embrace of her dark wings.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough, and a new scene. 'Nox ruit', 'night rushes on', falling fast; the phrase has a Homeric ring (Night 'swift' in Homer). 'fuscis… alis', 'with dusky wings', framing 'tellurem amplectitur': Night is pictured as a winged goddess. The verb 'amplectitur', 'embraces', prepares for the embrace of Venus and Vulcan that follows. Elision 'tellur(em) amplectitur'.

sentences.t:
At Venus haud animo nequiquam exterrita mater
Laurentumque minis et duro mota tumultu
Volcanum adloquitur thalamoque haec coniugis aureo
incipit et dictis divinum adspirat amorem:
sentences.l:
But Venus, not in mind without cause terrified, the mother,
both by the Laurentines' threats and by the harsh moved uproar,
Vulcan addresses, and in the bedroom these words of her husband, golden,
begins, and into her words divine breathes love:
sentences.i: But Venus, a mother with good cause for fear in her heart, alarmed by the threats of the Laurentines and their fierce uproar, turned to Vulcan, and in her husband's golden chamber began to speak, breathing divine love into her words:
sentences.n: 'At', marking the change of scene, from earth to heaven. 'haud… nequiquam', 'not in vain', 'not without reason', a double negative making a strong positive. 'animo… exterrita', 'terrified in mind'; 'mater', 'the mother', placed last: it is as Aeneas's mother that she is afraid. 'Laurentumque minis', 'by the threats of the Laurentines', 'Laurentum', genitive plural of 'Laurentes' (the shorter form of 'Laurentium'), the people of Latinus. 'duro… tumultu', 'by the harsh uproar', the call to arms of Book VII. 'Volcanum', Greenough's spelling of 'Vulcanum', the smith-god, Venus's husband; its 'a' is long, 'Vol-cā-num'. 'thalamo… coniugis aureo', 'in the golden chamber of her husband', framing 'haec'; 'aureo' is two syllables by synizesis, 'au-reo', and 'coniugis' is 'con-iu-gis', the 'i' a consonant. 'adspirat', Greenough's spelling of 'aspirat', 'breathes into', with dative 'dictis'. Elisions 'nequiqu(am) exterrita', 'Volcan(um) adloquitur', 'thalamoqu(e) haec', 'divin(um) adspirat'.

sentences.t:
“Dum bello Argolici vastabant Pergama reges
debita casurasque inimicis ignibus arces,
non ullum auxilium miseris, non arma rogavi
artis opisque tuae nec te, carissime coniunx,
incassumve tuos volui exercere labores,
sentences.l:
“While in war the Argive were laying waste Pergamum kings,
owed and destined to fall to hostile fires citadels,
not any help for the wretched, not arms did I ask
of your art and power, nor you, dearest husband,
or in vain your did I wish to put to work labours,
sentences.i: “While the Argive kings were laying waste to Pergamum in war, its towers doomed to fall to their enemies' fire, I asked for no help for those poor people, no weapons made by your skill and power; I would not set you, my dearest husband, or your labours, to work in vain,
sentences.n: Venus's speech opens (374–386): she asked no help when Troy fell. 'Dum… vastabant', 'while they were laying waste', 'dum' with the imperfect of a lasting action. 'Argolici… reges', 'the Argive kings', the Greek chiefs, enclosing 'vastabant Pergama'. 'Pergama', neuter plural, the citadel of Troy. 'debita', 'owed', due to fate; 'casuras… arces', 'citadels destined to fall', the future participle; 'inimicis ignibus', dative with 'casuras', or ablative of means. 'non ullum… non arma', anaphora. 'rogavi', 'I asked', with 'auxilium miseris', 'help for the wretched' (the Trojans), and 'arma artis opisque tuae', 'arms of your art and power'. 'nec te… incassumve tuos… exercere labores', 'nor (did I wish) to set you, or your labours, to work in vain': both 'te' and 'labores' are objects of 'exercere'. 'coniunx' is two syllables, 'con-iunx'. Elisions 'bell(o) Argolici', 'casurasqu(e) inimicis', 'ull(um) auxilium', 'volu(i) exercere'.

sentences.t:
quamvis et Priami deberem plurima natis
et durum Aeneae flevissem saepe laborem.
sentences.l:
although both to Priam I owed very much, to his sons,
and the hard of Aeneas I had wept for often labour.
sentences.i: though I owed so much to the sons of Priam, and had often wept over the cruel sufferings of Aeneas.
sentences.n: 'quamvis', 'although', with the subjunctive 'deberem' and 'flevissem'. 'Priami… natis', 'to Priam's sons', dative with 'deberem', framing 'deberem plurima', 'I owed very many things': Venus owed Troy a debt, since Paris, Priam's son, gave her the golden apple. 'durum… laborem', 'the hard toil', framing 'Aeneae flevissem saepe'; 'Aeneae', genitive, 'Ae-ne-ae', three syllables. 'labores… laborem', the same word ending 378 and 380, first Vulcan's work, then Aeneas's suffering. Elision 'dur(um) Aeneae'.

sentences.t: Nunc Iovis imperiis Rutulorum constitit oris:
sentences.l: Now by Jupiter's commands, of the Rutulians he has taken his stand on the shores:
sentences.i: Now, at Jupiter's command, he has set foot on the shores of the Rutulians;
sentences.n: 'Nunc', 'now', against the 'Dum' of 374. 'Iovis imperiis', 'by the commands of Jupiter', ablative of cause: Venus stresses that Aeneas is in Italy by Jupiter's will, not his own. 'constitit', 'has taken his stand', 'has settled', the subject Aeneas, from 380. 'Rutulorum… oris', 'on the shores of the Rutulians', Turnus's people, standing for Italy. No elisions.

sentences.t:
ergo eadem supplex venio et sanctum mihi numen
arma rogo genetrix nato.
sentences.l:
therefore I, the same, a suppliant come, and the holy to me power,
arms I ask, a mother for her son.
sentences.i: and so I, who never asked before, come as a suppliant to the divine power I hold sacred, and beg for arms, a mother for her son.
sentences.n: 'ergo', 'therefore'. 'eadem', 'the same (woman)', 'I who before asked nothing'. 'supplex venio', 'I come as a suppliant'. 'sanctum mihi numen', 'your power, holy to me', the person asked, with 'arma', the thing asked, both accusatives with 'rogo' (verbs of asking take two accusatives). 'genetrix nato', 'a mother for her son', the two words side by side, the plea in brief; 'nato', dative of advantage. Elisions 'erg(o) eadem', 'veni(o) et'.

sentences.t:
Te filia Nerei,
te potuit lacrimis Tithonia flectere coniunx.
sentences.l:
You the daughter of Nereus,
you could with tears the Tithonian bend, wife.
sentences.i: You let yourself be moved by the tears of Nereus's daughter, and of the wife of Tithonus.
sentences.n: 'Te… te', anaphora: 'you… you (were the one whom they could move)'. 'filia Nerei', 'the daughter of Nereus', Thetis, who got from Hephaestus (Vulcan) the arms of Achilles (Iliad 18). 'Nerei' is two syllables, 'Ne-rei', the '-ei' run together by synizesis. 'Tithonia… coniunx', 'the Tithonian wife', Aurora, the Dawn, wife of Tithonus, who got arms from Vulcan for her son Memnon; that story was told in the lost epic of the Trojan cycle, not in Homer (from memory). 'potuit… flectere', 'was able to bend (you)', singular with each subject. 'lacrimis', 'with tears', ablative of means. The argument is pointed: if Vulcan made arms for the sons of other wives, he can make them for his own wife's son. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Aspice qui coeant populi, quae moenia clausis
ferrum acuant portis in me exscidiumque meorum.”
sentences.l:
See what come together peoples, what walls with closed
sharpen steel gates against me and the destruction of my own.”
sentences.i: Look what peoples are gathering, what cities have shut their gates and are whetting the sword against me and the destruction of my own.”
sentences.n: 'Aspice', 'look', imperative. 'qui coeant populi', 'what peoples are coming together', and 'quae moenia… ferrum acuant', 'what walls are sharpening steel', indirect questions with the subjunctive. 'coeant' is three syllables, 'co-e-ant'. 'moenia', 'walls', for the cities they enclose. 'clausis… portis', ablative absolute, 'with gates closed', framing 'ferrum acuant'. 'in me', 'against me', Venus making her son's danger her own. 'exscidium', Greenough's spelling of 'excidium', 'destruction'. 'meorum', 'of my own', the Trojans. Venus's speech ends, and Greenough closes the mark. Elisions 'ferr(um) acuant', 'm(e) exscidiumque'.

sentences.t:
Dixerat et niveis hinc atque hinc diva lacertis
cunctantem amplexu molli fovet.
sentences.l:
She had spoken, and with snowy from this side and that, the goddess, arms
him hesitating, in an embrace soft she warms.
sentences.i: She had finished speaking; and as he hesitated, the goddess threw her snow-white arms about him on either side and warmed him in her soft embrace.
sentences.n: 'Dixerat', pluperfect, 'she had spoken', a common way to close a speech and move on. 'niveis… lacertis', 'with snowy arms', enclosing 'hinc atque hinc diva'. 'hinc atque hinc', 'on this side and on that', both arms about him. 'diva', 'the goddess'. 'cunctantem', 'him hesitating', object of 'fovet': Vulcan has not yet answered. 'amplexu molli', 'in a soft embrace', ablative of means. 'fovet', 'warms', 'cherishes', present tense, quickening the scene. Elisions 'atqu(e) hinc', 'cunctant(em) amplexu'.

sentences.t:
Ille repente
accepit solitam flammam, notusque medullas
intravit calor et labefacta per ossa cucurrit:
sentences.l:
He suddenly
received the accustomed flame, and the known the marrow
entered heat and through his loosened bones ran:
sentences.i: At once the flame he knew so well took hold of him; the familiar heat sank into his very marrow and ran through his melting frame:
sentences.n: 'Ille', 'he', Vulcan. 'repente', 'suddenly'. 'accepit solitam flammam', 'caught the accustomed flame', the fire of love, and fire is the smith-god's element. 'notus… calor', 'the familiar heat', framing 'medullas intravit', 'entered his marrow', the seat of passion in Latin love poetry. 'labefacta per ossa', 'through his loosened bones', 'labefacta' from 'labefacio', 'make to totter', 'weaken'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
non secus atque olim tonitru cum rupta corusco
ignea rima micans percurrit lumine nimbos.
sentences.l:
not otherwise than at times, when by thunder burst open, flashing,
a fiery rift, gleaming, runs through with light the storm-clouds.
sentences.i: just as sometimes a fiery rift, torn open by the flashing thunder, runs gleaming through the storm-clouds with its light.
sentences.n: A simile drawn from Vulcan's own element: lightning. 'non secus atque', 'not otherwise than', 'just as'. 'olim', 'at times', the use of 'olim' in similes for what happens now and then. 'tonitru… corusco', 'by the flashing thunder', ablative of cause, framing 'cum rupta': the thunder and lightning are one stroke. 'rupta', 'burst open', with 'ignea rima', 'a fiery crack', the lightning seen as a rift in the cloud. 'micans', 'flashing'. 'percurrit… nimbos', 'runs through the storm-clouds', 'lumine', 'with its light'. The flame of 389 is now a stroke across the sky. Elision 'atqu(e) olim'.

sentences.t: Sensit laeta dolis et formae conscia coniunx.
sentences.l: Felt it, glad in her wiles and of her beauty aware, the wife.
sentences.i: His wife felt it, pleased with her artful scheme and well aware of her beauty.
sentences.n: 'Sensit', 'she felt it', the effect of her embrace, placed first. 'laeta dolis', 'glad in her wiles', 'dolis' ablative of cause: the request was made with calculation. 'formae conscia', 'conscious of her beauty', 'formae' genitive with an adjective of knowing. 'coniunx', 'the wife', held to the end, as 'mater' at 370: Venus works as a wife on behalf of a son who is not her husband's. The scene recalls Hera's seduction of Zeus in Iliad 14 (from memory). No elisions.

sentences.t: Tum pater aeterno fatur devinctus amore:
sentences.l: Then the father with eternal speaks, bound fast, love:
sentences.i: Then the fire-god, bound fast by undying love, spoke:
sentences.n: 'pater', 'father', a title of honour for a god, as 'Ianus pater' at 357; here Vulcan (Mulciber, 'father Lemnius' elsewhere). 'aeterno… devinctus amore', 'bound fast by eternal love', framing 'fatur', 'speaks', ablative of means. 'devinctus', 'tied down', 'captivated', from 'devincio'. No elisions.

sentences.t: “Quid causas petis ex alto?
sentences.l: “Why reasons do you seek from the deep?
sentences.i: “Why do you go so far back for reasons?
sentences.n: Vulcan's reply opens here and runs to 404. 'causas', 'reasons', 'pleas', the arguments Venus has brought. 'ex alto', 'from the depth', 'from far off': her history of the Trojan war, her debt to Priam's sons, Thetis and Aurora. The question means 'you need not argue'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Fiducia cessit
quo tibi, diva, mei?
sentences.l:
Your confidence has gone
whither, goddess, in me?
sentences.i: Where has your trust in me gone, my goddess?
sentences.n: 'Fiducia… mei', 'confidence in me', 'mei' the objective genitive of 'ego', framing 'cessit quo tibi, diva'. 'quo', 'whither', 'to where', held back until after the subject and verb. 'tibi', dative of reference, 'for you', 'your'. 'cessit', 'has withdrawn', 'has gone'. 'diva', vocative, 'goddess', an affectionate address. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Similis si cura fuisset,
tum quoque fas nobis Teucros armare fuisset:
sentences.l:
Like if care had been,
then too right for us the Teucrians to arm it would have been:
sentences.i: Had you shown the same concern then, it would have been allowed me even then to arm the Trojans;
sentences.n: 'Similis si cura fuisset', 'if a like concern had been (yours)', the pluperfect subjunctive of a past unreal condition, and 'fas… fuisset', 'it would have been right', in the main clause: the same verb ends both lines. 'tum quoque', 'then too', at Troy. 'fas', 'what is allowed by divine law', with 'nobis', 'for us', the royal plural for 'me'. 'Teucros', 'the Teucrians', the Trojans, after their ancestor Teucer; Greek 'eu' is one syllable, 'Teu-cros'. 'armare', 'to arm', the business in hand. No elisions.

sentences.t:
nec pater omnipotens Troiam nec fata vetabant
stare decemque alios Priamum superesse per annos.
sentences.l:
neither the father all-powerful Troy nor the fates forbade
to stand, and ten other Priam to survive through years.
sentences.i: neither the almighty Father nor the fates forbade Troy to stand, or Priam to live on for ten years more.
sentences.n: 'nec… nec', 'neither… nor'. 'pater omnipotens', 'the almighty father', Jupiter. 'vetabant', imperfect, 'were not forbidding': the city's fall was fixed, but its date was not. 'Troiam… stare', 'Troy to stand', accusative and infinitive with 'vetabant'. 'decemque alios… per annos', 'through ten more years', framing 'Priamum superesse', 'Priam to survive'. Vulcan's claim is a bold one: fate could have been put off, though not undone, a view of fate the poem takes elsewhere too (Juno at 7.315). Elision 'decemqu(e) alios'.

sentences.t:
Et nunc, si bellare paras atque haec tibi mens est,
quidquid in arte mea possum promittere curae,
quod fieri ferro liquidove potest electro,
sentences.l:
And now, if to make war you are preparing, and this to you the mind is,
whatever in my art I can promise of care,
whatever made can be with iron or with molten electrum,
sentences.i: And now, if you are making ready for war and this is your purpose, whatever care I can promise in my craft, whatever can be wrought in iron or in molten electrum,
sentences.n: The sentence runs on to 404, with 'absiste' (403) as its main verb; it is split here because the last unit must also carry the narrative to 406 (the closing mark at 404 is joined to the next word). 'Et nunc', 'and now', against 'tum' at 397. 'si bellare paras', 'if you mean to make war'. 'haec tibi mens est', 'this is your mind', dative of possession, 'you have this purpose'. 'quidquid… curae', 'whatever of care', partitive genitive: 'all the care I can promise in my art'. 'quod fieri… potest', 'what can be made', 'with iron or molten electrum', ablatives of material. 'electrum', an alloy of gold and silver, also amber; here the metal. The line has a spondaic fifth foot, '-test ē-', before 'lec-trō'. These clauses are the objects of a promise left unstated. Elision 'atqu(e) haec'.

sentences.t:
quantum ignes animaeque valent, absiste precando
viribus indubitare tuis. ”Ea verba locutus
optatos dedit amplexus placidumque petivit
coniugis infusus gremio per membra soporem.
sentences.l:
as much as fires and breaths avail — cease by entreating
to doubt your strength.” These words having spoken,
the longed-for he gave embraces, and calm he sought,
of his wife poured into the lap, through his limbs, sleep.
sentences.i: all that fire and the breath of the bellows can achieve — stop doubting your power by pleading with me.” With these words he gave her the embrace she longed for, and, sinking into his wife's lap, let quiet sleep steal through all his limbs.
sentences.n: The print has 'tuis. ”Ea', with a space before the closing mark and none after it, a misprint for 'tuis.” Ea', corrected here; t keeps the print, because t must match the pinned source. Because the mark is joined to 'Ea', this unit also carries 'Ea verba locutus… soporem', as at 7.560 and 7.599. 'animae', 'breaths', the blasts of the bellows. 'absiste precando… indubitare', 'stop doubting your power by pleading': 'precando', the ablative of the gerund; 'indubitare', a rare verb, with the dative 'viribus… tuis' (L&S, from memory). Vulcan's speech ends. 'locutus', perfect participle of the deponent 'loquor'. 'optatos… amplexus', 'the longed-for embraces', framing 'dedit'. 'placidum… soporem', 'calm sleep', split across the lines. 'coniugis infusus gremio', 'poured into his wife's lap', 'gremio' dative with the compound participle. 'coniugis' is again 'con-iu-gis'. Elision 'quant(um) ignes'.
